Age, interest & context In the book: 6–9 months in the movement chapter; the authors also discuss awake back and tummy time in their 3–6 month section. Current self-initiated movement, interest, comfort and need for help. The age group is a way to browse; follow the interest or situation described here. Davies and Uzodike describe a prepared space where a baby can explore their own movements. A nearby object may invite a reach or a change of direction; the point is to follow the baby’s present interest and pace. Their caution is about propping a baby into sitting or standing. They separately describe awake time on both the back and tummy, while noticing discomfort and changing things or picking the baby up when needed. When effort turns to frustration, they describe coming closer and offering enough help for the baby to continue. Their activity ages are guides, and they explicitly welcome seeking support for developmental concerns. They describe asking for help when depleted, and seeking a doctor’s help for depression. In the everyday When looking after everyone else is leaving little room for you. The authors describe practical help as well as emotional company. A trusted friend, relative, partner if you have one, or another caregiver may be able to share some of the work. Paid help is one possibility when it is accessible. In The Montessori Baby, help can mean a meal or a household task so you can spend time with your baby. The authors suggest a visible list of useful jobs for visitors who want to help, especially when you are too tired to work out what to ask for. The Baby authors direct readers struggling with postpartum depression toward a doctor or trusted health professional. Davies also describes getting a doctor’s help when feeling depressed. These help-seeking passages sit alongside the books’ ordinary ideas for rest and support. What’s underneath Care for the adult is part of caring for the family.
